title: I stand at the gate and knock (Apocalypse 3:20)
word: I stand at the gate and knock
hookLine: if any man open the door, I will come in and sup with him

lines: A LANTERN AT A DARK DOOR.
cards: In the eighteen-fifties the English painter William Holman Hunt painted Christ at a door in a dark garden, holding a lantern and knocking. The door is overgrown with weeds and ivy; it hasn't been opened in a long time.
Prints of it hung in homes and churches, and people noticed something odd: the door has no handle on the outside.
The story goes that when someone pointed this out, Hunt said that was the point: this door can only be opened from within. He took the scene from one verse.

teach.b: "Behold, I stand at the gate, and knock. If any man shall hear my voice, and open to me the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me." That's the Douay-Rheims, with gate and door both.
Remember who hears it first. Not strangers who have never heard of Christ. Laodicea, the lukewarm church that said it needed nothing.
He has just rebuked them, because he loves them, and now the Lord of chapter one, with eyes like flame and the keys of death, waits on their doorstep, knocking.

teach.h: HE DOESN'T BREAK THE DOOR DOWN.
teach.b: He doesn't break the door down or climb in a window. The power is all on the inside: if any man hear, and open. Then the promise: sup with him.
The Greek word is the one for supper, the long evening meal at the end of work, where people actually talk. Not a quick visit at the door; a meal at your table.

Some readers hear an echo of the Song of Songs, where the beloved knocks at night and calls, open to me. For Catholics the line also points toward the altar, where Christ comes to his people in a meal.
And the promise is to any man, any one.
The church as a whole may be lukewarm; one person can still open.

teach.h: BEHOLD, I STAND AT THE GATE, AND KNOCK.
teach.b: Hunt painted a door that hadn't moved in years. That doesn't seem to discourage the one knocking.

how: Some Catholics pray with this verse in Eucharistic adoration and before Communion, and it is used at retreats and in invitations to return to the sacraments.

games.q: what does “i stand at the gate and knock” mean?
o: Christ forces his way in to rescue the lost
a warning that the door is shut now for good
Christ waits outside, and the door opens from within

games.q: the knock at the door — tap the pairs.
p: the lukewarm church he knocks for
painted the door with no outside handle

s: the verse is first spoken to people who had never heard of Christ
it's said to the church at Laodicea, a lukewarm congregation of believers.
in the verse, Christ forces his way in
he stands and knocks; the door is opened if any man hears and opens.
the promised meal is the main evening meal, not a quick visit
the Greek word means supper, the long meal at the end of the day.

games.q: you're at the door of a church that has gone lukewarm. you've rebuked them because you love them. no one has answered yet. what do you do?
o: keep standing and knocking, waiting for someone to open.
walk away and try another town.
games.why: behold, I stand at the gate, and knock. the power is on the inside: if any man shall hear my voice, and open to me the door, I will come in.

practice: Stand by a door with your hand on the handle, or picture your own front door. Think of a part of your life that's been closed a while, overgrown: a grief, a habit, a question about God you stopped asking.
Then open the door slowly, all the way, and leave it open for a few breaths; if you pray, let the opening be your prayer, and if not, just notice what it's like to open something on purpose.

wordCard.voice: I stand at the gate and knock. Apocalypse three: Christ waits outside, and the door opens from the inside. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: I will sup, eat the evening meal (Apocalypse 3:20), from deipnon, supper.

carryVoice: Your line: I stand and knock. And that's week eighty-nine: love the one you see, able to keep you, an unveiling, the first and the last, the first charity, not lukewarm, and I stand and knock. Week eighty-nine, done.
